answer: I'd like to talk about something you can see at almost every celebration in Bangladesh. An object of real cultural importance in my country is the traditional handloom sari, which carries deep significance. It is far more than a piece of clothing; it is a symbol of our heritage and identity. Woven by skilled artisans, each one is a genuine work of [[craftsmanship]], often taking days or even weeks to complete. The finest example is probably the jamdani, a delicate, almost transparent cotton sari whose weaving tradition has been recognised internationally. Women wear handloom saris at weddings, at Eid and especially at Pohela Boishakh, when the streets are full of red and white. They are also given as gifts at important family moments. I have known about it my whole life, having seen the women in my family wear them at every important occasion. My mother keeps a few folded carefully in her cupboard for special days, and since Sirajganj has a long tradition of handloom weaving, I've often seen weavers at work in nearby villages. What makes it so important is that it represents a centuries-old tradition that is sadly [[under threat]] from mass production. Wearing one on special days feels like honouring our [[ancestry]]. The intricate designs are genuinely [[exquisite]], and no two are ever identical. Honestly, I think it is vital that we protect such traditional crafts before they disappear. They connect us to our roots in a tangible way. I feel a real sense of pride whenever I see this beautiful item being worn and celebrated.

followUps.q: Have you ever bought a sari for someone?
followUps.answer: Yes, I bought a handloom sari for my mother last Eid. Choosing one was surprisingly difficult, because there were so many beautiful designs, but she loved the colour I picked.

followUps.q: Do young women in Bangladesh still wear saris?
followUps.answer: Yes, especially on special occasions like Pohela Boishakh and weddings. For everyday life, many prefer the salwar kameez, which is more practical, but the sari is still [[deeply cherished]].
